concepts.def: A characteristic a material shows regardless of applied forces, such as density, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity or absorbency.
How a material behaves when forces act on it or it is worked, including strength, hardness, toughness, elasticity and ductility.
A material's resistance to scratching, abrasion, wear and indentation; hard materials such as glass and tool steel resist surface damage.
The ability of a material to absorb impact energy and withstand sudden shocks without cracking or shattering; the opposite of brittleness.
The visual and tactile qualities of a material, such as colour, texture and surface pattern, that influence how appealing a product looks and feels.
The price of a material, the stock forms it is supplied in and how easily it can be sourced all affect whether a design is viable.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Material Considerations — a core area of GCSE Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Material Considerations brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Material Considerations.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A material that resists scratching and wear is described as:
options: Tough
Hard
Ductile
Malleable
The ability to absorb impact energy without fracturing
Resistance to scratching
The ability to conduct electricity
The ability to be stretched into wire

mcqs.q: Which of these is a physical property rather than a working property?
options: Tensile strength
Hardness
Thermal conductivity
Toughness
Shattered easily by impact
Compressed but never stretched
Hammered only into flat sheets
Drawn out into thin wire without breaking

mcqs.q: Is a hard material always a tough material?
options: Yes - if a material is hard it must also be tough.
No - hardness and toughness are different properties; glass is hard but brittle, so it shatters under impact.
Yes - hardness and toughness are two names for the same property.
Hardwood means wood that has been painted or treated.

mcqs.q: Are all hardwoods physically harder than all softwoods?
options: Density is an aesthetic property because it affects appearance.
Yes - hardwood means the wood is always harder than softwood.
No - the terms describe the tree type, broadleaved deciduous versus coniferous; balsa is a hardwood yet very soft.
Hardwood means wood that has been painted or treated.

mcqs.q: Is density a working property of a material?
options: Density is an aesthetic property because it affects appearance.
No - density is a physical property; working properties describe how a material responds to forces, such as strength or toughness.
Yes - hardness and toughness are two names for the same property.
Yes - every measurable property of a material is a working property.
